title: Adaptive Attacks Break Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM Agents

object.carrier: none — the paper evaluates single-turn IPI attack/defense interactions (agent executes the user tool, reads one tool response, next one or two outputs are judged); no persistent memory, skill, experience, or shared state is formed, stored, or reused across turns/tasks

safety_property.statement: Protects LLM agents from indirect prompt injection: malicious instructions embedded in tool responses must not make the agent execute attacker-chosen tools (integrity: unauthorized actions such as financial transactions or device control) or exfiltrate sensitive user data (confidentiality: data stealing). The property fails when the agent's output executes the attacker tool; judged per test case by tool-execution match, not keyword or LLM judgment.
safety_property.operationalized_as: ASR on InjecAgent: success = output includes execution of the attacker tool Ta (direct harm); for data stealing, step 1 = executes the data extraction tool, step 2 (with gpt-4-0613 simulating the tool response) = executes the data transmission tool. ASR-all = successful attacks / total test cases (default); ASR-valid also defined over valid outputs. Detector defenses are additionally scored by detection rate (DR).

capabilities: Injects a malicious instruction Ia into the external content ETu of a tool response (e.g., an email or review) that the agent reads; the attacker cannot directly modify the agent's prompt, tools, or model
Appends/prepends optimized adversarial strings to the malicious instruction (GCG, Multi-objective GCG, Two-stage GCG, AutoDAN) to force execution of the attacker tool Ta

Adaptive attacks assume knowledge of and white-box access to the agent model, defense models, and detailed prompts; joint or iterative optimization against the specific defense (e.g., stealth objective to fool detectors, two-stage strings to survive paraphrasing, low-perplexity AutoDAN strings)
assumptions: IPI setting: the attacker can only manipulate the content of external sources the agent accesses
White-box access to agent and defense models and prompts for adaptive string optimization (stated as the adaptive-attack standard)
Single turn of interaction is evaluated: the agent executes the user tool, retrieves the response, and its next one or two outputs are judged; success = execution of the attacker tool
Defenses are deployed individually and their mechanism is fully disclosed to the attacker before the attack is crafted
not_covered: Black-box and grey-box attackers (authors flag this as future work)
Combinations of multiple defenses deployed together
Impact of defenses and attacks on normal/benign cases (utility under no attack) — explicitly not assessed
Exhaustive coverage of all potential IPI defenses (e.g., LLM self-evaluation, alternative finetuning methods)
Attacks targeting multi-step/long-horizon behavior beyond the agent's first-step action

intervention.name: Stress-test of eight existing IPI defenses (fine-tuned detector, LLM-based detector, perplexity filtering, instructional prevention, data prompt isolation, sandwich prevention, paraphrasing, adversarial finetuning) with per-defense adaptive attacks; no new defense proposed
intervention.description: The paper contributes the attack side: adapting jailbreak attack strategies (GCG, M-GCG, T-GCG, AutoDAN) to IPI with knowledge of each defense. The evaluated defenses span content-level detection (DeBERTaV3 classifier, LLM Yes/No prompt, perplexity threshold), input/prompt-level content modification (warning instructions, ''' delimiters, repeated user command, paraphrasing), and one model-level defense (adversarial finetuning via LoRA on unsuccessful attacks), so mechanism_layer is recorded as content (7 of 8 defenses are content-level).

limitations.statement: Adaptive attacks focus solely on the agent's first-step action: all adversarial strings are trained to produce the ReAct-style first-step output ('Thought: I will use the {Attacker tool name} tool to,'), so improvement on the second step of data-stealing attacks is minimal; refining attacks for longer-term impact is left to future work.
